'''''Ageratina riparia''''', commonly known as '''mistflower''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]], native to [[Mexico]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Turner|first=Billie Lee|title=The Comps of Mexico: A systematic account of the family Asteraceae|date=1997|series=Phytologia Memoirs|pages=i–iv, 1–272|chapter=Eupatorieae|issue=11}}</ref><ref>{{Tropicos|2709250|Ageratina riparia|(Regel) R.M. King & H. Rob.}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Ageratina riparia|url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=36478#null|access-date=2022-12-15|website=[[ITIS]]}}</ref> The species is widely [[Adventive plant|adventive]] and has spread to [[Cuba]], [[Jamaica]], and other parts of the [[Caribbean]]. It has also been introduced as an [[ornamental plant]] and naturalized in a variety of regions, including parts of [[Hawaii]], [[South Africa]], [[Southeast Asia]], [[Macaronesia]], [[Oceania]], [[Peru]], and the [[Indian subcontinent]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Ageratina riparia|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/7013-2?_gl=1*n1uapp*_ga*MTM0NDkxNTY4OC4xNjcxMDk3NjM4*_ga_ZVV2HHW7P6*MTY3MTA5NzcyNS4xLjEuMTY3MTA5ODk5MS4wLjAuMA..|access-date=15 December 2022|website=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]]}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|date=21 November 2022|title=Ageratina riparia|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomydetail?id=317712|access-date=15 December 2022|website=GRIN-Global|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]}}</ref> In tropical climates, ''A. riparia'' is highly [[Invasive species|invasive]] and a variety of control methods have been developed to reduce its spread.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last1=Ratnayake|first1=R.M.N.D.|last2=Bandara|first2=B.M.R.|last3=Adikaram|first3=N.K.B.|last4=Wijesundara|first4=D.S.A.|last5=Karunaratne|first5=V.|date=2018|title=Potential of the antifungal activity of Ageratina riparia (Regel) R. M. King and H. Rob. against banana anthracnose disease caused by the fungus, Colletotrichum musae|journal=[[Ceylon Journal of Science]]|volume=47|issue=3|pages=287|doi=10.4038/CJS.V47I3.7536 |s2cid=92485020 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Fröhlich|first1=J.|last2=Fowler|first2=S.V.|last3=Gianotti|first3=A.|last4=Hill|first4=R.L.|last5=Killgore|first5=E.|last6=Morin|first6=L.|last7=Sugiyama|first7=L.|last8=Winks|first8=C.|display-authors=1|date=2000|editor-last=Spencer|editor-first=Neal R.|title=Biological Control of Mist Flower (''Ageratina riparia'', Asteraceae): Transferring a Successful Program from Hawai'i to New Zealand|journal=Proceedings of the X International Symposium on Biological Control of Weeds|publisher=[[Montana State University]]|pages=51}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
The species was identified by [[Eduard August von Regel|Eduard Regel]] as ''Eupatorium riparium'' in the 1866 edition of [[Gartenflora]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Regel|first=Eduard|author-link=Eduard August von Regel|date=1866|title=Eupatorium riparium Hort.|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/40084699#page/358/mode/1up|journal=[[Gartenflora]]|language=de|volume=15|pages=324–340|via=[[Biodiversity Heritage Library]]}}</ref> It was given its current classification as member of the genus [[Ageratina]] by [[R.M. King|Robert Merrill King]] and [[Harold E. Robinson]] in a 1970 edition of [[Phytologia]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=King|first1=R.M.|last2=Robinson|first2=Harold Ernest|author-link2=Harold E. Robinson|date=1970|title=Studies in the Eupatorieae (Compositae) XIX. New combinations in Ageratina|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/13020678|journal=[[Phytologia]]|volume=19|pages=210|via=[[Biodiversity Heritage Library]]}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Ageratina riparia (Regel) R. King & H. Rob.|url=https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/5TS9X|access-date=2022-12-15|website=[[Catalogue of Life]]}}</ref> The species has several [[heterotypic synonym]]s, including: ''Ageratina repens'', ''Ageratina ventillana'', ''Eupatorium harrisii'', ''Eupatorium ventillanum'', and ''Fleischmannia repens''.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Robinson|first=B.L.|author-link=Benjamin Lincoln Robinson|date=October 1918|title=Diagnoses and Notes Relating to Tropical American Eupatorieae|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/20025755.pdf|journal=Proceedings of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences |publisher=[[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]|volume=54|issue=4|pages=262–263|doi=10.2307/20025755 |jstor=20025755|jstor-access=free}}</ref>

The name ''Ageratina'' is derived from [[Greek language|Greek]] meaning "un-aging", in reference to the way the plant's flowers keep their color for an extended period of time. This name was used by [[Dioscorides]] for a number of different plants.<ref name="gledhill">{{Cite book|last=Gledhill|first=David|title=The Names of Plants|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|year=2008|isbn=9780521685535|page=39|language=en}}</ref> The name ''riparia'' is derived from the [[Latin]] word ''ripa'' meaning "riverbank"' or "streambank". The suffix ''-aris'' denotes that it "belongs to" the bank. Thus, ''riparia'' means 'growing on the banks'.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|title=Ageratina riparia|url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/ageratina-riparia/|access-date=2022-12-15|website=[[New Zealand Plant Conservation Network]]|language=en}}</ref>

A wide variety of [[common name]]s exist for the plant. In English it has been referred to as '''creeping croftonweed''', '''mistflower''', '''river-eupatorium''', '''spreading snakeroot''', and '''William Taylor'''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jung|first1=Ming-Jer|last2=Hsu|first2=Tian-Chuan|last3=Chung|first3=Shih-Wen|last4=Peng|first4=Ching-I|date=2009|title=Three Newly Naturalized Asteraceae plants in Taiwan|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/242586601|journal=[[Taiwania]]|language=en|volume=54|issue=1|pages=76|via=[[ResearchGate]]}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> In [[KwaZulu-Natal]], it may be called '''mistblom'''.<ref name=":3" /> In Hawaii, the plant is commonly referred to as '''hāmākua pāmakani'''.<ref>{{Cite web|date=12 April 2013|title=Ageratina riparia|url=http://www.hear.org/pier/species/ageratina_riparia.htm|access-date=2022-12-15|website=Hawaiian Ecosystems at Risk Project}}</ref> The term ''pāmakani'' means "windblown" in the [[Hawaiian language]], referring to the way its seeds are naturally dispersed.<ref name=":9">{{Cite book|last1=Davis|first1=Clifton J.|url=http://www.hear.org/books/apineh1992/pdfs/apineh1992iv1davisetal.pdf|title=Alien Plant Invasions in Native Ecosystems of Hawaii: Management and Research|last2=Yoshioka|first2=Ernest|last3=Kageler|first3=Dina|publisher=[[University of Hawaii Press]]|year=1992|isbn=0-8248-1474-6|editor-last=Stone|editor-first=Charles P.|pages=425–426|language=en|chapter=Biological Control of Lantana, Prickly Pear, and Hamakua Pamakani in Hawai'i: a Review and Update|editor-last2=Smith|editor-first2=Clifford W.|editor-last3=Tunison|editor-first3=J. Timothy}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Ageratina riparia (Los Tilos) 03.jpg|thumb|Flowers of ''A. riparia'' on [[La Palma]], [[Canary Islands]].]]
Mistflower is a low growing, sprawling [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] that may grow up to 1 meter in height in some climates.<ref name=":1" /> The species has a fibrous rootstock and its stems are often woody and covered in purple hairs.<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tripathi|first1=Radhey Shyam|last2=Yadav|first2=A.S.|last3=Kushwaha|first3=Satya P.S.|date=2006|title=Ecology of Three Invasive Species of Eupatorium: A Review|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/287739758|journal=International Journal of Ecology and Environmental Sciences|volume=32|issue=4|pages=301–302|via=[[ResearchGate]]}}</ref> The stems may produce additional roots if they contact the ground.<ref name=":8" />

The [[serrated]] [[Leaf|leaves]] on average reach 7.5 cm long and 2.5 cm wide and taper at each end. The leaves form in opposing pairs which are coarsely serrated except near the base.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":8" /> The species is related to and closely resembles ''[[Ageratina adenophora]]''. However, its distinctive serrated leaves may be used to distinguish mistflower from ''A. adenophora''.<ref name=":8" /> The white flowers are also similar in appearance to ''A. adenphora''.<ref name=":13" /> The [[flower]]s are white with dense heads at the ends of the branches. Mistflower buds from July until August, and may flower from August through March in some climates.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":8" /> Its [[seed]]s are black, slender, angular, 2 mm long, with fine white hairs at the tip. They are [[Seed dispersal|dispersed]] by wind and flowing water. Mature plants can produce around 10,000 to 100,000 seeds per year.<ref name=":10">{{Cite book|last=Gunasekera|first=Lalith|title=Invasive Plants: A guide to the identification of the most invasive plants of Sri Lanka|publisher=Colombo|year=2009|isbn=9780646514895|pages=107–108}}</ref><ref name=":15">{{Cite journal|last1=Zancola|first1=Brian J.|last2=Wild|first2=Clyde|last3=Hero|first3=Jean-Marc|date=24 December 2001|title=Inhibition of Ageratina riparia (Asteraceae) by native Australian flora and fauna|journal=[[Austral Ecology]]|volume=25|issue=5|pages=563–569 |doi=10.1046/j.1442-9993.2000.01087.x}}</ref>

== Distribution and invasiveness ==
Mistflower is native to western Mexico. In its natural habitat the flower occurs sparsely and may even be considered endangered. Specimens were originally collected from the canyon of El Mirador, Mexico in 1857 for use as an [[ornamental plant]]. It was then brought back to Germany by [[Jean Jules Linden]]. From Linden's specimen, mistflower was introduced to many parts of the globe as an ornamental plant during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal|last=Trujillo|first=Eduardo E.|date=1985|title=Biological Control of Hamakua Pa-Makani with Cercosporella sp. in Hawaii|url=https://www.invasive.org/proceedings/pdfs/6_661-671.pdf|journal=Proceedings of the Sixth International Symposium on Biological Control of Weeds, 19–25 August 1984|page=662}}</ref>

Outside of its natural habitat, the species spread quickly. It has become naturalized in many regions, including parts of [[South Africa]], [[tropical Asia]], [[Oceania]], [[Macaronesia|Macronesia]], [[Madagascar]], the [[Mascarenes]], [[Hawaii]], and [[Peru]]. Mistflower has become especially invasive in tropical and warm temperate climates.<ref name=":1" /> In these regions, the species can form dense [[underbrush]]. The branches of mistflower plants may intertwine with each other, creating a blanket effect which out-competes native flora and prevents indigenous species from propagating because of the lack of sunlight.<ref name=":15" /><ref name=":11">{{Cite journal|last1=Barton|first1=Jane|last2=Fowler|first2=Simon V.|last3=Gianotti|first3=Alison F.|last4=Winks|first4=Chris J.|last5=de Beurs|first5=Maarten|last6=Arnold|first6=Greg C.|last7=Forrester|first7=Guy|date=March 2007|title=Successful biological control of mist flower (Ageratina riparia) in New Zealand: Agent establishment, impact and benefits to the native flora|journal=[[Biological Control]]|volume=40|issue=3|pages=370–385|doi=10.1016/j.biocontrol.2006.09.010}}</ref><ref name=":12" /> In [[Sri Lanka]], for example, it chokes out native plants in the country's mountain and cloud forests, and in [[pasture]]s, [[Embankment (earthworks)|roadsides]], [[Barren lands|barren areas]] and [[bushland]]s of other places where it has been introduced with often disastrous effects.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gunasekera|first=Lalith|date=23 October 2011|title=Invaders In Knuckles Mountain Range|work=[[Sri Lanka Guardian]]|url=http://www.srilankaguardian.org/2011/10/invaders-in-knuckles-mountain-range.html|access-date=19 June 2016}}</ref> There is evidence that mistflower's decaying [[plant matter]] further inhibits the [[Seed germination|germination]] of native flora as it produces [[Allelopathy|allelopathic compounds]] in decomposition that limit soil nutrients.<ref name=":15" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rai|first1=J.P.N.|last2=Tripathi|first2=R.S.|date=1984|title=Allelopathic effects of Eupatorium riparium on population regulation of two species of Galinsoga and soil microbes|journal=[[Plant and Soil]]|volume=80|pages=105–117 |doi=10.1007/BF02232944|s2cid=35519724 }}</ref> It also adversely affects grazing [[pasture]]s, as it can be [[Toxicity|toxic]] to horses and is often avoided by grazing stock.<ref name=":11" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=O'Sullivan |first1=B.M. |title=Plant Toxicity: Proceedings of the Australian-U.S.A. Poisonous Plants Symposium, Brisbane, Australia |last2=Gibson |first2=J.A. |last3=MacKenzie |first3=R.A. |publisher=Queensland Poisonous Plants Committee |year=1985 |isbn=9780724213177 |pages=423–426 |language=en}}</ref>

Outside of its natural habitat, mistflower is often found in temperate pastoral areas and wetlands. The species grows in either sun or shade, but prefers higher levels of light found in marginal habitats: at the edge of forests and on streambanks.<ref name=":15" /> It thrives in warm and humid habitats, especially subtropical and tropical forests.<ref name=":11" /><ref name=":8" /> Mistflower is tolerant to most soils, variable humidity levels, shade, and is resilient to damage from grazing.<ref name=":8" />

==Control==
[[File:Mist Flower Smut Entyloma ageratinae.jpg|thumb|Close-up of the underside of a leaf infected by ''[[Entyloma ageratinae]]'' in [[Auckland]].]]Because of mistflower's broadly invasive nature, a variety of methods to control its spread have been developed by various countries since the mid-20th century. Mechanical measures are often employed against the plant, such as attempts to uproot areas overtaken by the plant. A variety of herbicides are currently employed against ''A. riparia'', including: [[dicamba]], [[glyphosate]], [[Metsulfuron-methyl|metsulfuron]], [[aminopyralid]], [[metsulfuron-methyl]], [[triclopyr]], [[fluroxypyr]], [[picloram]], and [[aminopyralid]].<ref name=":13">{{Cite web|date=2020|title=Mistflower: Ageratina riparia|url=https://www.daf.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0011/72866/mistflower.pdf|access-date=15 December 2022|website=[[Queensland Government]]|publisher=[[Department of Agriculture and Fisheries (Queensland)|State of Queensland, Department of Agriculture and Fisheries]]}}</ref>

=== Biological control agents ===
A number of biological control agents have been identified for use against ''A. riparia'' in regions where the species is invasive. These include, the gall fly ''[[Procecidochares alani]]'', the plume moth ''[[Hellinsia beneficus]]'', and the smut fungus ''[[Entyloma ageratinae]]''.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal|last1=Rupasinghe|first1=P.A.|last2=Gunaratne|first2=A.M.T.A.|date=2017|title=Impacts of Ageratina riparia (Regel) R.M. King and H. Rob. on natural regeneration of sub-montane forests at Knuckles Forest Reserve, Sri Lanka|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/321799627|journal=[[Ceylon Journal of Science]]|volume=46|issue=4|pages=85–96|doi=10.4038/cjs.v46i4.7471 |via=[[ResearchGate]]|doi-access=free}}</ref> All of these species damage existing plants or otherwise inhibit its ability to propagate.

[[Entyloma ageratinae|''Entyloma Ageratinae'']], a [[smut fungus]], has been one of the most successful agents employed against the species.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Manual of Biocontrol Agents|publisher=[[British Crop Production Council]]|year=2004|isbn=9781901396355|editor-last=Copping|editor-first=Leonard G.|edition=3rd|location=Alton, UK|language=en|ol=16147289M}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Wood|first=Alan|date=July–September 2009|title=Weed Research: Leaf smut appears to have controlled mistflower in KwaZulu-Natal|journal=Plant Protection News|publisher=Plant Protection Research Institute|volume=81|pages=13}}</ref><ref name="baroon">{{cite web|last=|title=Restoring biodiversity in NSW through biocontrol of mistflower|url=http://www.lbccg.org.au/restoring-biodiversity-in-nsw-through-biocontrol-of-mistflower/|access-date=3 March 2014|website=Lake Baroon Catchment Care Group}}</ref> The species of fungus is commonly known as mist flower smut as it is highly specific to mist flower plants. In 1974, specimens of ''E. Ageratinae'' were intentionally collected from mistflower plants in Jamaica, where it was noticed that mistflower was not as invasive as other regions with a similar climate. After a number of [[host range]] studies, proved that the pathogen only posed a threat to mistflower plants, the fungus was released at three sites on Oahu in 1975. One of these sites saw the area previously covered by mistflower drop from ~75% to less than 1% within 9 months, allowing for indigenous plants to reemerge. Following the fungus' proven success in several other inoculations were made at other sites throughout Hawaii. The pathogen spread quickly, especially in moist areas of the islands.<ref name=":14" /> After the pathogen's success in Hawaii, ''E. ageratinae'' was introduced at nine sites in New Zealand in 1998. The fungus quickly spread across the islands, quickly infecting an estimated 60% of live mistflower leaves.<ref name=":11" />

''[[Hellinsia beneficus]],'' a [[Plume Moth|plume moth]] from Mexico, was collected for the control of ''A. riparia'' because its larvae feed on the species' leaves.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Conant|first=Patrick|date=1998|title=Scientific Note: A New Host Record for Oidaematophorus beneficus Yano & Happner (Lepidoptera: Pterophoridae)|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/5104762.pdf|journal=[[Hawaiian Entomological Society|Proceedings of the Hawaiian Entomological Society]]|volume=33|pages=151|via=[[CORE (research service)|CORE]]}}</ref> Unsuccessful attempts were made to introduce the species to Hawaii in 1959 and 1965.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last1=Yano|first1=Kôji|last2=Heppner|first2=John B.|date=15 October 1983|title=Description of Hamakua pamakani Plume Moth from Hawaii (Lepidoptera: Pterophoridae)|url=https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/e124621a-fe59-4564-afb2-1850db5998ff/content|journal=[[Hawaiian Entomological Society|Proceedings of the Hawaiian Entomological Society]]|volume=24|issue=2 & 3|pages=335–341|via=[[University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa|Scholar Space]]}}</ref> The moth was successfully introduced in Hawaii in 1973 when a total of approximately 1525 specimens were released at [[Kaʻala|Mt. Kaala]] and [[Kona, Hawaii|Kona]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nakao|first1=H.K.|last2=Funasaki|first2=G.Y.|last3=Davis|first3=C.J.|date=1975|title=Introductions for Biological Control in Hawaii, 1973|url=https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/5c1b83ad-cbab-4836-8a1d-1ba972b4dee6/content|journal=[[Hawaiian Entomological Society|Proceedings of the Hawaiian Entomological Society]]|volume=22|issue=1|pages=109–111|via=[[University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa|Scholar Space]]}}</ref> The moth prefers higher altitudes and has rarely been observed below 1500 ft. by researchers in Hawaii. However, the moth has been effective in controlling ''A. riparia'' by damaging its leaves at elevations between 1500 ft and 4000 ft.<ref name=":6" />[[File:Starr-180305-0575-Ageratina riparia-stem galls biocontrol-Kahikinui-Maui (27363332858).jpg|thumb|Stem galls caused by ''[[Procecidochares alani]]'' on [[Maui]], [[Hawaii]].]]''[[Procecidochares alani]]'', a [[Gall-inducing insect|gall fly]], spends its larval stage within the stem of mistflower plants, causing the formation of a bulbous gall at the top of the stem.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hapai|first1=Marlene N.|last2=Chang|first2=Franklin|date=March 1986|title=The Induction of Gall Formation in Ageratina riparia by Procecidochares alani (Diptera: Tephritidae). I. Gall Histology and Internal Gross Morphology of the Third Instar|url=https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/f379a97c-0eef-403a-85f7-c1bbed434d7a/content|journal=[[Hawaiian Entomological Society]]|volume=26|via=[[Semantic Scholar]]}}</ref> This gall slows the plant's growth and inhibits its ability to compete with surrounding flora. The species is highly specific to the mistflower plant and poses little threat to other flora.<ref name=":1" /> Specimens were collected from Mexico by William Rose in 1973 as a potential biocontrol agent to be used in Hawaii.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":14" /> The fly was first released at Kona in 1974, followed by several other locations on the island of [[Hawaii (island)|Hawaii]]. Together, the moth ''P. alani'' and the fly ''H. beneficus'' have helped control mistflower populations in high altitude areas of Hawaii where the smut fungus ''E. ageratina'' has not already devastated the population.<ref name=":9" /> Following the success of ''P. alani'' in controlling mistflower in Hawaii, the species was introduced to Australia in 1987 and to New Zealand in 2001.<ref name=":15" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Paynter|first1=Quentin|last2=Fowler|first2=Simon V.|last3=Groenteman|first3=Ronny|date=2018|title=Making weed biological control predictable, safer and more effective: perspectives from New Zealand|journal=[[BioControl]]|volume=63|issue=3 |pages=431|doi=10.1007/s10526-017-9837-5|s2cid=254290604 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In Australia, ''P. alani'', but failed to establish itself as a biocontrol agent as it was soon effected by native [[parasitoid wasp]]s.<ref name=":15"/> The species had greater success in New Zealand.

A total of 11,630 flies were released in New Zealand across 34 sites in 2001. Compared to ''E. ageratinae'', which had been released in New Zealand two years prior, ''P. alani'' had a more limited effect. The gall fly population did grow exponentially at release sites, but was comparatively slow to spread across New Zealand.<ref name=":11" /> The gall fly, however, has been proven to be more effective at targeting mistflower plants in dry areas, while the fungus ''E. ageratinae'' prefers moist habitats.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Denslow|first1=Julie S.|last2=D'Antonio|first2=Carla M.|date=December 2005|title=After biocontrol: Assessing indirect effects of insect releases|journal=[[Biological Control]]|volume=35|issue=3|pages=313|doi=10.1016/j.biocontrol.2005.02.008}}</ref> The two species are therefore most effective acting together to control mistflower populations.<ref>{{Cite web|date=8 August 2020|title=Who's Who in Biological Control of Weeds?|url=https://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/publications/weed-biocontrol/weed-biocontrol-articles/status-of-agents/|access-date=15 December 2022|website=[[Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research]]}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Mistflower has most commonly been used as an [[ornamental plant]]. It may also be harvested for use as a [[Tanning (leather)|tanning]] agent.{{Citation needed|date=December 2022}} In some regions, it is used for the stabilization of embankments and for partitioning land.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ageratina riparia (Regel) R.M. King & H. Robins.|url=https://mansfeld.ipk-gatersleben.de/apex/f?p=185:46:15645051654456::NO::module,mf_use,source,akzanz,rehm,akzname,taxid:mf,,botnam,0,,Ageratina%20riparia,33048|access-date=2022-12-15|website=Mansfeld's World Database of Agricultural and Horticultural Crops|publisher=[[Leibniz Institute]] of Plant Genetics and Crop Plant Research}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Sengupta|first1=Rabishankar|last2=Sekhar Dash|first2=Sundhansu|date=2020|title=Invasion Status of Three Non-Native Species from Family Asteraceae in Mizoram|url=https://nelumbo-bsi.org/index.php/nlmbo/article/view/153742/106916|journal=Nelumbo|language=en|volume=62|issue=1|pages=31|doi=10.20324/nelumbo/v62/2020/153742|s2cid=238905774 |issn=2455-376X|url-access=subscription|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Near the village of [[Sangau]] in [[India]] where the species is known as ''Hlo-thar'', there is evidence of the use of the plant's dried leaves and flowers to prepare an [[herbal tea]], taken to reduce [[Hypertension|blood pressure]] and [[Blood sugar level|blood sugar]].<ref name=":5" />

The production of a methanol extract using the aerial part of the plant has revealed that the plants contain the antifungal compound [[methylripariochromene]]. Research into the antifungal aspects of mistflower suggest that its components may be exploited to create a [[fungicide]] able to control ''[[Colletotrichum musae|Colletotruchum musae]]'', the cause of banana anthracnose disease.<ref name=":7" />
